analysis.one_liner: Restores EPA's duty to protect health and blocks unlawful deregulation under the Clean Air Act.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2026 with 4 Democratic cosponsors and referred to five House committees, none of which has taken it up.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Environmental Protection Agency to resume its core mission of protecting human health and the environment, roll back deregulatory actions the bill calls unlawful, and require the agency to enforce the Clean Air Act [S1]. In practice, that means stronger federal air-pollution rules and enforcement against polluters, and fewer rollbacks of existing protections [S1]. The bill was introduced in the House in September 2026 and sent to five committees, but none has acted on it [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe polluted air — particularly residents near power plants, refineries, industrial facilities, and busy highways — would gain if stronger Clean Air Act enforcement restores and tightens pollution limits. Communities that bear a disproportionate share of industrial pollution stand to benefit most, as would state and local air agencies that rely on an actively enforcing EPA.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities exposed to industrial air pollution

how_it_helps.text: The bill would restore and strengthen the EPA's legal obligation to protect human health and the environment, the mission the agency exists to carry out [S1].
It would halt deregulatory actions the bill identifies as unlawful, stopping rollbacks of existing pollution protections before they take full effect [S1].

It would require the EPA to enforce the Clean Air Act, meaning more active policing of air pollution from power plants, refineries, and industrial facilities rather than looser limits and weaker oversight [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, electric utilities, and industrial facilities would bear the cost of tighter pollution limits, monitoring, and enforcement, including possible penalties for violations. Some of those compliance costs could be passed to consumers through energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Stronger Clean Air Act enforcement means real compliance costs for power plants, refineries, and manufacturers, and those costs can be passed on to households through higher energy and goods prices; the affected industries argue the recent deregulatory actions were lawful, not unlawful, so the bill's premise would likely be tested in court.

The bill frames EPA's recent actions as unlawful and directs the agency to reverse course, which would invite litigation over whether the agency's deregulation violated its legal duties — a fight that could delay the health protections the bill aims to restore.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential public health gains from restored Clean Air Act enforcement are large and well-documented in the record of what the bill targets. The costs fall on polluting industries, though some compliance costs would reach consumers through energy prices. The bill's main weakness is that it does nothing to resolve its own premise: it assumes EPA's deregulatory actions were unlawful, a question only the courts can settle, and litigation could stall the very protections it orders.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five House committees when it was introduced in September 2026, and none of them has held a hearing or a vote, so it is still sitting in committee while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Casten introduced the bill on September 17, 2026, with four Democratic cosponsors [S1][S2].

The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee plus four others — Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, Natural Resources, and Science, Space, and Technology — splitting its provisions among them [S3].
No committee has taken further action since the referral, and the bill has received no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, industries that would face tighter pollution limits and enforcement are better off, because the bill has not advanced past its initial committee referrals.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controls committee agendas and House floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: The bill's referral to five committees ended in no action from any of them, and the chamber has given it no hearing or vote

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 4 cosponsors are House Democrats, with no Republican support recorded; there has been no vote to show a fuller breakdown [S2].

industries.note: Restored Clean Air Act enforcement would mean tighter limits, more monitoring, and penalties for pollution from fossil fuel extraction and combustion. The industry's interest in continued deregulation runs against the air-quality protections the bill offers the public.
Power plants, especially coal- and gas-fired ones, would face stricter emission limits and enforcement. Some compliance costs would reach households through electricity rates.
Industrial facilities would face renewed air-pollution rules and EPA enforcement actions that recent deregulation had relaxed.

analysis.trajectory: The House is controlled by Republicans and no Republican has supported the bill, and referrals to five committees make it easy for any single panel to let it sit. It has had no committee action since September 2026, so the most likely path is that it stays in committee and dies when this Congress ends in January 2027.
